newsitem.title: UK: Major ignores polls on eve of British election.
newsitem.headline: Major ignores polls on eve of British election.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Wednesday ignored polls showing his Conservatives heading for a crushing defeat in Britain's election, saying he was optimistic his party's economic achievements could guarantee victory.
But it seems almost everyone else in Britain expects the Labour Party under Tony Blair to sweep to power on Thursday, ending 18 years of Conservative rule that has transformed society.
An NOP/Reuters opinion poll released 17 hours before voting began showed the Conservatives lagging 22 points behind Labour, riding high on the support of 50 percent of the electorate.

Bookmakers said they had stopped taking bets on a Labour victory and Major's finance minister Kenneth Clarke, eternally optimistic throughout the six-week campaign, turned his attention to the consequences of defeat for the first time.
Major, the figurehead of his party's campaign, remained unprepared to countenance defeat, returning to a favourite theme that voters cannot trust Labour on economic policy.
"No one can honestly question that the transformation in Britain has been anything less than an economic miracle. It's too good to give up," he told the campaign's final news conference.
"It would be a tragedy if these opportunities were lost by the false atraction of a well-packaged marketing scam," Major said in reference to Labour's slick, no-risks campaign.
Major dismissed the opinion polls, which wrongly forecast he would lose the last election in 1992.
"I don't share their opinion...that we're going to lose tomorrow. I think this election is there to be won. There are huge numbers of people who are undecided," Major told BBC radio.

The NOP/Reuters poll points to Labour winning more than 440 seats in the 659-seat parliament, the biggest majority since 1924. But analysts think such a victory is unlikely because of the vagaries of Britain's first-past-the-post electoral system.
In the four elections since Labour last held power in 1979, the Conservatives have not polled more than 44 percent of the vote.
Blair, whose party last won an election in 1974, was also cautious about the result and urged Britain's 44 million voters to come out and vote Labour to avoid a fifth successive Conservative term.
Blair, who calls himself the "eternal warrior against complacency", told supporters in northeast England: "It's there, it can be done. With your support we can do it.
"Let us together tomorrow come out, support the Labour Party, build that better Britain and give our children the future they need."
Blair has revitalised Labour since becoming leader in July 1994 by dragging it from the left to the political centre.
A leading firm of bookmakers said it had stopped taking bets on Labour gaining the most seats at the May 1 election.
William Hill said it took the decision after the odds on Labour winning most seats fell to just 1-12, the point where punters would pay more in tax than they would get in winnings.

The last time the firm closed its books on an election was in 1979, when the Conservatives swept to power under Margaret Thatcher and began the longest unbroken stretch of one-party rule in the 20th century.
A Conservative win on Thursday would arguably be the biggest political sensation since 1945, when voters threw out wartime prime minister Winston Churchill in a Labour landslide.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Clarke broke the unwritten rule of not mentioning defeat, warning the ruling party against tearing itself apart after a Labour victory.

Clarke, who has fought a rearguard action from the cabinet to slow the party's drift to a more right-wing, anti-European stance, told Sky News: "I think the people who turn afterwards to post mortems and scapegoating will make us look ridiculous.

"I have been in parties which have lost elections and the thing to do is pick yourself up and work out how you are going to win the next one and that is not by having internecine warfare and recriminations."
Labour's lead has been steady for two years and has held up since Major called the election on March 17, hoping to wear Labour down with the longest campaign for more than 80 years.
No party has ever come back from such a deficit to win. This time Labour needs a vote swing of 4.3 percent from the Conservatives over 1992 figures to win an overall majority.

Support for the minority Liberal Democrats is also firm at around 15 percent compared to Labour's 50 and the Conservatives' 30 percent. The Liberal Democrats could hold the balance of power if neither Labour nor the Conservatives gain a majority.
